case.title: Brownfield provider leakage
case.problem_statement: Qwen built-in voice knowledge appears in frontend, preflight, workflow, and root composition.
case.desired_outcome: Put voice discovery under one clear owner and reduce coordinated provider changes.
expected_future_changes: A second provider may be added.

confirmed_facts.text: A provider interface exists but does not own voice discovery.

clusters.title: Provider Refactoring and Extensibility
clusters.rationale: The investigation must address the current risk where fragmented metadata ownership (F1) and high structural change propagation in the provider module (F2) create a fragile dependency network, which directly threatens the ability to add a second provider (F3) without replicating existing leakage patterns.

findings.text: The constant 'BUILT_IN_VOICES' is explicitly defined in at least three separate modules: provider (node_a318f9ng90ef44a374deb), preflight (node_92a4630788576ec9b367ceeb), and frontend (node_536006b74f276f558fddf482).

The fragmentation of voice discovery knowledge across the module boundary increases the risk that adding a second provider will require coordinated, error-prone updates to the preflight and frontend logic.
The provider module (node_a318f9f739ea4d81cd5c8088) exhibits high structural impact, with a reverse dependency reach of 5 and a fan-in of 4.

The current dependency density of the provider module acts as a bottleneck for extensibility; any attempt to implement the second required provider will likely amplify changes across the entire system unless the interface and discovery mechanism are decoupled from the component values.
A static call target in 'workflow.narrate' (node_198cbab990e7a6018996a618) for 'provider.synthesize' could not be resolved.

implications: High risk of architectural fragility: The current pattern of leaking provider-specific constants (BUILT_IN_VOICES) into consumer modules makes the system vulnerable to desynchronization during provider expansion.
Reduced development velocity: Adding a new provider will require high-effort, multi-module changes due to existing structural dependencies and duplicated metadata.

design_forces.title: Distributed Voice Metadata Ownership
design_forces.description: The responsibility for defining and accessing built-in voice information (e.g., `BUILT_IN_VOICES`) is currently fragmented across the `provider`, `preflight`, and `frontend` modules.
design_forces.importance_rationale: This fragmentation is the primary driver of the current 'leakage' problem; without centralized ownership, adding new capabilities requires coordinated changes across multiple disconnected boundaries.

design_forces.title: High Change Propagation in Provider Module
design_forces.description: The `provider` module exhibits high structural impact, with a high likelihood of affecting up to 5 downstream modules during changes.
design_forces.importance_rationale: Because the provider is a significant dependency bottleneck (high fan-in and reverse reach), any refinement to its interface or logic forces widespread coordination and increases regression risk.

design_forces.title: Second Provider Extensibility Pressure
design_forces.description: The system must accommodate the introduction of an additional provider without replicating existing discovery logic in upstream modules.
design_forces.importance_rationale: While not yet a realized change, this future requirement makes the current leakage of discovery logic into `preflight` and `frontend` a significant architectural debt that will prevent localized implementation.

alternatives.title: Preserve Current Distributed State
alternatives.summary: Maintain the existing pattern of duplicating 'BUILT_IN_VOICES' across the provider, preflight, and frontend modules.

alternatives.title: Delegate Discovery to Provider Interface
alternatives.summary: Refactor the 'VoiceProvider' interface to include a method for retrieving available voices (e.g., `get_available_voices()`), moving responsibility from consumers back to the provider implementation.

alternatives.title: Introduce Centralized Provider Registry
alternatives.summary: Create a dedicated registry or metadata module that aggregates voice information from all active providers, allowing consumers to query a single source of truth.

assumptions: A second provider implementation will be introduced with its own unique set of capabilities and voice metadata.
The existing requirement for 'BUILT_IN_VOICES' to be available in preflight and frontend logic remains a functional necessity.

alternative_results.alt_status_quo_fragmented_constants: High risk of architectural fragility. Adding a second provider will necessitate coordinated, manual updates to the 'provider', 'preflight', and 'frontend' modules to synchronize 'BUILT_IN_VOICES'. This increases the probability of desynchronization errors across the module boundaries (as evidenced by claim_671553e2267c4a77b7decc2a5fe79ca5).
alternative_results.alt_interface_delegation_discovery: Moderate improvement in decoupling. Moving discovery to `get_available_voices()` within the `VoiceProvider` interface eliminates the need for consumers to maintain duplicated constants (addressing the signal 'similarly-named-constant'). However, it still relies on consumers having access to a specific provider instance, which does not fully address the high reverse dependency reach (5) of the provider module.
alternative_results.alt_centralized_registry_metadata: Optimal for long-term extensibility. By introducing a centralized registry, the system achieves the highest degree of decoupling. Consumers query a single source of truth, which minimizes change amplification across the 'preflight' and 'frontend' modules when new providers are added, directly addressing the structural bottleneck identified in node_a318f9f739ea4d81cd5c8088.

scenarios.conclusion: Advisor inference: Alternative A3 is recommended to minimize coordinated change and reduce the risk of desynchronization during provider expansion, though it introduces a new architectural component (the registry).

policy.title: Keep each architectural fact in one authoritative place
policy.body:
## Intent
Prevent one conceptual change from requiring synchronized edits.
## Guidance
Consolidate duplicated rules, mappings, and capability knowledge under their natural owner.
## Signals
The same list, constant, validation rule, or conditional appears in unrelated modules.
## Diagnostic questions
Are these copies accidental, cached, or intentionally independent?
## Likely consequences
Changes become atomic and contradictory definitions are less likely.
## Exceptions
Deliberate denormalization is valid when synchronization and ownership are explicit.
## Positive example
Built-in voices are declared by the provider and consumed by preflight and presentation.
## Counterexample
Unrelated code is merged merely because two fragments happen to look alike.
## Related policies
See `explicit-source-of-truth` and `assign-clear-ownership`.

chunks.text: Built-in voices are declared by the provider and consumed by preflight and presentation.

policy.title: Define interfaces around stable concepts, not incidental mechanisms
policy.body:
## Intent
Keep short-lived implementation choices from shaping long-lived application contracts.
## Guidance
Name domain capabilities and results independently from the first provider or framework.
## Signals
Public interfaces contain vendor names, transport fields, or framework lifecycle objects.
## Diagnostic questions
Would this concept still exist if the current implementation were replaced?
## Likely consequences
Contracts change for domain reasons rather than adapter churn.
## Exceptions
Provider-specific features may remain explicitly provider-specific when portability is not a goal.
## Positive example
`VoiceCatalog` represents an application capability while Qwen owns its construction.
## Counterexample
Renaming every concrete object to `Generic*` without changing its semantics.
## Related policies
See `contain-dependencies` and `keep-interfaces-simple`.

chunks.text: `VoiceCatalog` represents an application capability while Qwen owns its construction.

policy.title: Hide implementation details behind the owning boundary

source.author: ArchCompass
inspiration: John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design

policy.body:
## Intent
Prevent callers from depending on decisions that belong to another module.
## Guidance
Expose the capability a caller needs while keeping formats, provider rules, and algorithms private.
## Signals
Several callers reproduce the same internal rule or inspect an implementation-specific type.
## Diagnostic questions
Which decisions can the module change without coordinating with callers?
## Likely consequences
Callers become simpler and implementation changes affect fewer locations.
## Exceptions
Transparent data types are appropriate when their representation is the stable shared concept.
## Positive example
A provider returns a voice catalog without exposing how its built-in voices are discovered.
## Counterexample
A wrapper forwards every provider option and therefore hides nothing.
## Related policies
See `assign-clear-ownership` and `contain-dependencies`.

chunks.text: A provider returns a voice catalog without exposing how its built-in voices are discovered.

policy.title: Keep one conceptual change local
policy.body:
## Intent
Reduce coordinated edits caused by a single decision.
## Guidance
Group knowledge that changes together while separating responsibilities that change independently.
## Signals
Adding one provider requires changes in presentation, validation, workflow, and root composition.
## Diagnostic questions
Which files change together, and is there one responsibility behind those edits?
## Likely consequences
Feature changes touch fewer locations and partial updates become less likely.
## Exceptions
Cross-cutting security or compliance changes may intentionally affect many boundaries.
## Positive example
Adding a provider requires one adapter and one composition registration.
## Counterexample
A large central module is justified only because all changes are now in one file.
## Related policies
See `avoid-duplicated-knowledge` and `contain-dependencies`.

chunks.text: Adding one provider requires changes in presentation, validation, workflow, and root composition.

policy.title: Compare two materially different designs before committing

source.author: ArchCompass
inspiration: John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design (2nd ed.)

policy.body:
## Intent
Avoid mistaking the first workable decomposition for the best design when a decision is consequential or difficult to reverse.
## Guidance
Sketch at least two materially different allocations of responsibility or interfaces, then compare information hiding, interface complexity, change locality, failure modes, and fit with credible future changes before choosing.
## Signals
The first plausible design is accepted without alternatives, ownership remains debatable, or discussion focuses on implementation detail before module boundaries are tested.
## Diagnostic questions
What fundamentally different design could satisfy the same needs, and which comparison criteria would reveal a meaningful advantage?
## Likely consequences
Hidden assumptions surface earlier, trade-offs become explicit, and the selected design has a reason stronger than familiarity or momentum.
## Exceptions
Do not manufacture alternatives for a small, reversible change with an established local precedent, or when an urgent incident requires a temporary containment fix.
## Positive example
Before adding model-based report questions, compare provider-owned prompt assembly, application-owned context assembly, and a dedicated conversation domain service against the same evidence and evolution scenarios.
## Counterexample
Two alternatives differ only in class names while keeping the same responsibilities, dependencies, and public interface.
## Related policies
See `assign-clear-ownership`, `optimize-locality-of-change`, and `delay-premature-abstraction`.

policy.title: Make important relationships explicit and discoverable
policy.body:
## Intent
Help maintainers find dependencies, ownership, and configuration without relying on hidden convention.
## Guidance
Represent important relationships in types, composition, names, or queryable metadata.
## Signals
Behavior depends on import side effects, naming coincidences, or undocumented registration.
## Diagnostic questions
How would a new maintainer locate and verify this relationship?
## Likely consequences
Unknown unknowns decrease and structural evidence becomes more reliable.
## Exceptions
Well-established language conventions need not be restated everywhere.
## Positive example
Provider registration occurs in one visible composition root.
## Counterexample
Importing an unrelated module silently mutates a global registry.
## Related policies
See `explicit-source-of-truth` and `apply-consistency-deliberately`.
